questions.question: A binary composition $*$ is defined on $R\times R$ by $(a,b)*(c,d)=(ac,bc+d)$, where $a,b,c,d\in R$. Find $(2,3)*(1,-2)$.
questions.answer:
Apply the definition $(a,b)*(c,d)=(ac,\ bc+d)$ with $(a,b)=(2,3)$ and $(c,d)=(1,-2)$:

$$(2,3)*(1,-2)=\left(2\times1,\ 3\times1+(-2)\right)$$

$$=(2,\ 3-2)=(2,\ 1)$$

$$\therefore\ (2,3)*(1,-2)=(2,1)$$

Note the two components behave quite differently: the first is the product $ac$, the second is $bc+d$ — the second entry of the first pair times the first entry of the second pair, plus the second entry of the second pair.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\sin\left\{\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right)\right\}$.
questions.answer:
The range of $\sin^{-1}$ is $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, and $\sin^{-1}$ is **odd**: $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$. Since $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac12$,

$$\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right)=-\sin^{-1}\frac12=-\frac{\pi}{6}$$

Therefore

$$\sin\left\{\frac{\pi}{3}-\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right\}=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\sin\frac{\pi}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ \sin\left\{\frac{\pi}{3}-\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right)\right\}=1$$

The whole point is the double negative: subtracting a negative inverse returns $+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, giving the familiar angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.question: Find the values of $a$ and $b$ for which $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\-a&2b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5\\4\end{bmatrix}$.
questions.answer:
Perform the matrix product on the left, then equate corresponding entries:

$$\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\-a&2b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2a-b\\-2a-2b\end{bmatrix}$$

So we need

$$2a-b=5\qquad\ldots(1)$$

$$-2a-2b=4\qquad\ldots(2)$$

Adding (1) and (2):

$$(2a-b)+(-2a-2b)=5+4\ \Rightarrow\ -3b=9\ \Rightarrow\ b=-3$$

Substituting $b=-3$ in (1): $2a+3=5\Rightarrow 2a=2\Rightarrow a=1$.

$$\therefore\ a=1,\qquad b=-3$$

**Check:** $\begin{bmatrix}1&-3\\-1&-6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2+3\\-2+6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5\\4\end{bmatrix}$ ✓.

questions.topic: Constructing a Matrix from a Formula
questions.question: Construct a $2\times2$ matrix whose $(i,j)^{th}$ element is given by $a_{ij}=\dfrac{2i-j}{3}$.
questions.answer:
A $2\times2$ matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\a_{21}&a_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ has four elements; substitute the row and column indices into $a_{ij}=\dfrac{2i-j}{3}$.

**First row** ($i=1$):

$$a_{11}=\frac{2(1)-1}{3}=\frac13,\qquad a_{12}=\frac{2(1)-2}{3}=0$$

**Second row** ($i=2$):

$$a_{21}=\frac{2(2)-1}{3}=\frac33=1,\qquad a_{22}=\frac{2(2)-2}{3}=\frac23$$

Therefore

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}\frac13 & 0\\[2pt] 1 & \frac23\end{bmatrix}$$

Every entry is obtained by the same rule — noting that $a_{12}=0$ exactly because $2i-j=2-2=0$ when $i=1,\ j=2$.

questions.question: Show that $x=1$ is a root of the equation $\begin{vmatrix}x+1&2x&1\\2x&x+1&-4\\-3&4x-7&6\end{vmatrix}=0$.
questions.answer:
Apply the column operation $C_1\to C_1-C_2$, which leaves the determinant unchanged:

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}(x+1)-2x & 2x & 1\\ 2x-(x+1) & x+1 & -4\\ -3-(4x-7) & 4x-7 & 6\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\begin{vmatrix}1-x & 2x & 1\\ x-1 & x+1 & -4\\ 4-4x & 4x-7 & 6\end{vmatrix}$$

Each entry of the first column now contains the factor $(x-1)$; take it out:

$$\Delta=(x-1)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2x & 1\\ 1 & x+1 & -4\\ -4 & 4x-7 & 6\end{vmatrix}$$

Since $\Delta=0$ is the given equation, and the second factor is (in general) a number,

$$x-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=1$$

$$\therefore\ x=1\ \text{is a root of the given equation}\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Check directly:** putting $x=1$,

$$\begin{vmatrix}2&2&1\\2&2&-4\\-3&-3&6\end{vmatrix}$$

has its first two columns identical, so the determinant vanishes at once ✓.

questions.question: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=x^3-2x+8$ at the point $(1,7)$.
questions.answer:
The **slope of the tangent** at a point is the derivative evaluated there. Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^3-2x+8\right)=3x^2-2$$

At $x=1$:

$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=1}=3(1)^2-2=3-2=1$$

$$\therefore\ \text{slope of the tangent}=1$$

**Check the point lies on the curve:** $y(1)=1-2+8=7$ ✓. A slope of 1 means the tangent there is the line $y-7=1(x-1)$, i.e. $y=x+6$.

questions.question: Using the properties of determinants, prove that $\begin{vmatrix}a-b-c&2a&2a\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}=(a+b+c)^3$.
questions.answer:
*(The statement of Q.11 on the source scan is destroyed; it is recovered from the solution printed immediately below it, which carries out exactly this reduction.)*

Take the determinant and apply the row operation $R_1\to R_1+R_2+R_3$ (determinant unchanged):

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}a+b+c & a+b+c & a+b+c\\ 2b & b-c-a & 2b\\ 2c & 2c & c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

because

$$(a-b-c)+2a+2a=a+b+c$$

$$2b+(b-c-a)+2b=a+b+c$$

$$2c+2c+(c-a-b)=a+b+c$$

**Take out the common factor $(a+b+c)$ from the first row:**

$$\Delta=(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

**Apply $C_1\to C_1-C_2$ and $C_2\to C_2-C_3$:**

$$\Delta=(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 & 1\\ 2b-(b-c-a) & (b-c-a)-2b & 2b\\ 2c-2c & 2c-(c-a-b) & c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\ a+b+c & -(a+b+c) & 2b\\ 0 & a+b+c & c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

**Take out $(a+b+c)$ from the first and the second column:**

$$\Delta=(a+b+c)^3\begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\1&-1&2b\\0&1&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

**Expand along the first row** — only the entry $1$ in column 3 survives, with cofactor sign $(-1)^{1+3}=+1$:

$$\Delta=(a+b+c)^3\cdot1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=(a+b+c)^3\left[(1)(1)-(-1)(0)\right]=(a+b+c)^3\cdot1$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}a-b-c&2a&2a\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}=(a+b+c)^3\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Check:** $a=b=c=1$ gives $\begin{vmatrix}-1&2&2\\2&-1&2\\2&2&-1\end{vmatrix}=27=3^3$ ✓.

questions.question: If the following function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$, find the value of $a$: $f(x)=\dfrac{1-\cos4x}{x^2}$ for $x<0$; $f(x)=a$ for $x=0$; $f(x)=\dfrac{a\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{16+\sqrt{x}}-4}$ for $x>0$.
questions.answer:
For continuity at $x=0$ we need the two one-sided limits and $f(0)$ to agree.

**Left-hand limit** ($x\to0^-$). Use $1-\cos4x=2\sin^22x$:

$$\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{1-\cos4x}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{2\sin^22x}{x^2}=2\lim_{x\to0^-}\left(\frac{\sin2x}{x}\right)^2$$

Since $\dfrac{\sin2x}{x}\to2$:

$$=2\times(2)^2=2\times4=8$$

So the left limit is $8$.

**Right-hand limit** ($x\to0^+$). Rationalise the denominator by multiplying by the conjugate $\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}+4$:

$$\frac{a\sqrt x}{\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}-4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}+4}{\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}+4}=\frac{a\sqrt x\left(\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}+4\right)}{\left(16+\sqrt x\right)-16}$$

$$=\frac{a\sqrt x\left(\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}+4\right)}{\sqrt x}=a\left(\sqrt{16+\sqrt x}+4\right)$$

Letting $x\to0^+$:

$$\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=a\left(\sqrt{16}+4\right)=a(4+4)=8a$$

**Apply continuity.** Continuity at $0$ requires

$$\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=f(0)$$

$$8=8a=a\ \Rightarrow\ a=1$$

$$\therefore\ a=1$$

With $a=1$ all three quantities equal $8$, so $f$ is continuous at $x=0$.

questions.question: If $x=a\sin2t(1+\cos2t)$ and $y=b\cos2t(1-\cos2t)$, prove that at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{b}{a}$.
questions.answer:
Differentiate each function with respect to $t$ using the product rule.

**For $x$:** $x=a\sin2t+a\sin2t\cos2t$.

$$\frac{dx}{dt}=a(2\cos2t)+a\left[2\cos2t\cdot\cos2t+\sin2t(-2\sin2t)\right]$$

$$=2a\cos2t+2a\cos^22t-2a\sin^22t$$

$$=2a\cos2t+2a\cos4t$$

**For $y$:** $y=b\cos2t-b\cos^22t$.

$$\frac{dy}{dt}=-2b\sin2t-b\cdot2\cos2t(-2\sin2t)=-2b\sin2t+4b\sin2t\cos2t$$

$$=-2b\sin2t+2b\sin4t$$

**At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:** here $2t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $4t=\pi$, so

$$\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0,\qquad \cos\pi=-1,\qquad \sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1,\qquad \sin\pi=0$$

$$\left.\frac{dx}{dt}\right|_{t=\pi/4}=2a(0)+2a(-1)=-2a$$

$$\left.\frac{dy}{dt}\right|_{t=\pi/4}=-2b(1)+2b(0)=-2b$$

Therefore

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\frac{-2b}{-2a}=\frac{b}{a}$$

$$\therefore\ \left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{t=\pi/4}=\frac{b}{a}\qquad\blacksquare$$

The two minus signs cancel, which is why the result is $+\dfrac ba$ and not $-\dfrac ba$.

questions.question: A stone is dropped into a quiet lake and the waves move in circles. If the radius of a circular wave increases at the rate of 5 cm/sec, find the rate of increase of its area at the instant when its radius is 8 cm.
questions.answer:
**Set up the variables.** Let $r$ be the radius and $A$ the area of the circular wave at time $t$. Then

$$A=\pi r^2$$

**Differentiate with respect to $t$** (chain rule, since $r$ depends on $t$):

$$\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\,\frac{dr}{dt}$$

**Given:** $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=5$ cm/sec, and we want $\dfrac{dA}{dt}$ when $r=8$ cm. Substituting:

$$\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi(8)(5)=80\pi$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{dA}{dt}=80\pi\ \text{cm}^2/\text{sec}\approx251.3\ \text{cm}^2/\text{sec}$$

So the area is growing at $80\pi$ cm²/sec — i.e. about $251$ cm² per second — at the moment the radius passes 8 cm. Note the rate grows with $r$: the same 5 cm/sec expansion adds more area when the circle is already large.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{e^x}{\sqrt{5-4e^x-e^{2x}}}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Put $t=e^x$, so $dt=e^x\,dx$ (which is exactly the numerator):

$$I=\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt{5-4t-t^2}}$$

Complete the square inside the root:

$$5-4t-t^2=-\left(t^2+4t-5\right)=-\left[(t+2)^2-9\right]=9-(t+2)^2$$

So

$$I=\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt{3^2-(t+2)^2}}$$

This is the standard form $\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{a^2-u^2}}=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{u}{a}+C$ with $u=t+2$ and $a=3$:

$$I=\sin^{-1}\frac{t+2}{3}+C$$

Back-substituting $t=e^x$:

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{e^x}{\sqrt{5-4e^x-e^{2x}}}\,dx=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{e^x+2}{3}\right)+C$$

**Check by differentiating:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{e^x+2}{3}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{(e^x+2)^2}{9}}}\cdot\dfrac{e^x}{3}=\dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{9-(e^x+2)^2}}=\dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{5-4e^x-e^{2x}}}$ ✓.

questions.topic: Definite Integral of an Even-Type Integrand
questions.question: Prove that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx=\pi$.
questions.answer:
First quote the standard property: if $f(a-x)=f(x)$, then

$$\int_0^{a}x\,f(x)\,dx=\frac{a}{2}\int_0^{a}f(x)\,dx$$

*(This follows from $I=\int_0^a xf(x)dx=\int_0^a(a-x)f(a-x)dx=\int_0^a(a-x)f(x)dx$, so $2I=a\int_0^af(x)dx$.)*

Here $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}$ and

$$f(\pi-x)=\frac{1}{1+\sin(\pi-x)}=\frac{1}{1+\sin x}=f(x)$$

so with $a=\pi$:

$$I=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}dx=\frac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}$$

Now evaluate the remaining integral. Multiply by $\dfrac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x}$:

$$\frac{1}{1+\sin x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin^2x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x-\sec x\tan x$$

$$\int_0^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}=\left[\tan x-\sec x\right]_0^{\pi}$$

$$=\left(\tan\pi-\sec\pi\right)-\left(\tan0-\sec0\right)$$

$$=\left(0-(-1)\right)-\left(0-1\right)=1+1=2$$

Therefore

$$I=\frac{\pi}{2}\times2$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx=\pi\qquad\blacksquare$$

(The antiderivative $\tan x-\sec x$ has a removable singularity at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$; splitting the integral there and taking limits confirms the value $2$.)

questions.question: Find the intervals in which the function $f(x)=(x-1)(x-2)^2$, $x\in R$ is (a) increasing, (b) decreasing.
questions.answer:
**Expand and differentiate.**

$$f(x)=(x-1)\left(x^2-4x+4\right)=x^3-4x^2+4x-x^2+4x-4$$

$$=x^3-5x^2+8x-4$$

$$f'(x)=3x^2-10x+8$$

**Factorise the derivative.** Split $-10x$ as $-6x-4x$:

$$3x^2-6x-4x+8=3x(x-2)-4(x-2)=(3x-4)(x-2)$$

So $f'(x)=(3x-4)(x-2)$, which vanishes at $x=\dfrac43$ and $x=2$.

**Sign of $f'$ on the three intervals:**

| Interval | Sign of $(3x-4)$ | Sign of $(x-2)$ | Sign of $f'$ | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x<\dfrac43$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | increasing |
| $\dfrac43<x<2$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ | decreasing |
| $x>2$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | increasing |

**(a) Increasing on**

$$\left(-\infty,\ \frac43\right)\cup\left(2,\ \infty\right)$$

**(b) Decreasing on**

$$\left(\frac43,\ 2\right)$$

So $x=\dfrac43$ is a local maximum and $x=2$ a local minimum. Since $f(x)\to\pm\infty$ at the ends, these are only local extrema.

questions.topic: Modulus, Dot Product, Cross Product, Projection
questions.question: If $\vec a=\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k$ and $\vec b=2\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, then find the following: (i) $|\vec a|$ (ii) $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ (iii) $\vec a\times\vec b$ (iv) the projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$.
questions.answer:
**(i) Modulus of $\vec a$.**

$$|\vec a|=\sqrt{1^2+(-3)^2+4^2}=\sqrt{1+9+16}=\sqrt{26}$$

$$|\vec a|=\sqrt{26}\approx5.099$$

**(ii) Dot product.**

$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(1)(2)+(-3)(1)+(4)(1)=2-3+4=3$$

$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$$

**(iii) Cross product.**

$$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-3&4\\2&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(-3)(1)-(4)(1)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(1)-(4)(2)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(1)-(-3)(2)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(-3-4)-\hat j(1-8)+\hat k(1+6)$$

$$=-7\hat i+7\hat j+7\hat k=7\left(-\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\right)$$

$$\vec a\times\vec b=-7\hat i+7\hat j+7\hat k$$

**(iv) Projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec b$.**

$$\text{proj}_{\vec b}\vec a=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2+1^2}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt6}$$

$$\text{proj}_{\vec b}\vec a=\frac{3}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\approx1.225$$

**Check the cross product:** $(-7\hat i+7\hat j+7\hat k)\cdot\vec a=-7-21+28=0$ ✓ and $\cdot\vec b=-14+7+7=0$ ✓.

questions.question: The position vectors of the two points A and B are $\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$ and $\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ respectively. Find the vector equation of the plane passing through B and perpendicular to AB.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the normal.** The plane is perpendicular to $AB$, so $\vec{AB}$ is its normal vector:

$$\vec{AB}=\vec{OB}-\vec{OA}=\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)-\left(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\right)=-2\hat j$$

So a normal to the plane is $\vec n=-2\hat j$, equivalently $\hat j$.

**Step 2 — point–normal form.** The vector equation of the plane through the point with position vector $\vec b=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$ and normal $\vec n$ is

$$\left(\vec r-\vec b\right)\cdot\vec n=0$$

Taking $\vec n=-2\hat j$:

$$\left(\vec r-\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)\right)\cdot(-2\hat j)=0$$

Expanding:

$$\vec r\cdot(-2\hat j)+\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)\cdot(2\hat j)=0$$

$$\vec r\cdot(-2\hat j)+2=0\ \Rightarrow\ \vec r\cdot\hat j=1$$

$$\therefore\ \vec r\cdot\hat j=1$$

**In Cartesian form** this is simply $y=1$ — as expected, since $AB$ is parallel to the $y$-axis and the plane through $B(1,-1,1)$ perpendicular to it is the horizontal plane $y=-1$. Using the normal $\vec{AB}=-2\hat j$ directly:

$$\vec r\cdot(-2\hat j)=\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)\cdot(-2\hat j)=2$$

$$\therefore\ \vec r\cdot\hat j=-1,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad y=-1$$

**The plane is $y=-1$**, written vectorially as $\vec r\cdot\hat j=-1$.

questions.question: If A and B are two independent events such that $P(A)=0.35$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.6$, find $P(B)$.
questions.answer:
For **independent** events, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. The addition rule gives

$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$$

Substituting $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$:

$$P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)$$

With $P(A)=0.35$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.6$:

$$0.6=0.35+P(B)-0.35\,P(B)$$

$$0.6=0.35+0.65\,P(B)$$

$$0.65\,P(B)=0.25$$

$$P(B)=\frac{0.25}{0.65}=\frac{25}{65}=\frac{5}{13}$$

$$\therefore\ P(B)=\frac{5}{13}\approx0.385$$

**Check:** $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{7}{20}\cdot\dfrac{5}{13}=\dfrac{7}{52}$, and $\dfrac{7}{20}+\dfrac{5}{13}-\dfrac{7}{52}=\dfrac{91+100-7}{260}=\dfrac{184}{260}=0.6$ ✓.

questions.topic: Inverse by Elementary Row Operations / Matrix Method
questions.question: Using elementary row transformations, find the inverse of $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&3&-2\\-3&0&-1\\2&1&0\end{bmatrix}$. / Or, solve by matrix method: $2x-y+z=2$, $x+y-z=1$, $4x+y+2z=7$.
questions.answer:
**First part — inverse by row operations.** Write $A=I A$ and reduce $A$ to $I$, applying each operation to the right-hand block as well:

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&3&-2&1&0&0\\-3&0&-1&0&1&0\\2&1&0&0&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_2\to R_2+3R_1$, $R_3\to R_3-2R_1$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&3&-2&1&0&0\\0&9&-7&3&1&0\\0&-5&4&-2&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_2\to\frac19R_2$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&3&-2&1&0&0\\0&1&-\frac79&\frac13&\frac19&0\\0&-5&4&-2&0&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_3\to R_3+5R_2$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&3&-2&1&0&0\\0&1&-\frac79&\frac13&\frac19&0\\0&0&\frac19&-\frac13&\frac59&1\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_3\to9R_3$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&3&-2&1&0&0\\0&1&-\frac79&\frac13&\frac19&0\\0&0&1&-3&5&9\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_2\to R_2+\frac79R_3$, $R_1\to R_1+2R_3$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&3&0&-5&10&18\\0&1&0&-2&4&7\\0&0&1&-3&5&9\end{array}\right]$$

**$R_1\to R_1-3R_2$:**

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&0&0&1&-2&-3\\0&1&0&-2&4&7\\0&0&1&-3&5&9\end{array}\right]$$

$$\therefore\ A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&-3\\-2&4&7\\-3&5&9\end{bmatrix}$$

**Check:** $A A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&3&-2\\-3&0&-1\\2&1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&-3\\-2&4&7\\-3&5&9\end{bmatrix}$ gives row 1: $(1-6+6,\ -2+12-14,\ -3+21-18)=(1,0,0)$ ✓, and similarly for the other rows.

**Or — matrix method.** The system $2x-y+z=2$, $x+y-z=1$, $4x+y+2z=7$ is

$$\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&1\\1&1&-1\\4&1&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\7\end{bmatrix}$$

$$|A|=2(2+1)-(-1)(2+4)+1(1-4)=6+6-3=9\ne0$$

**Cofactors:**

$$C_{11}=2+1=3,\quad C_{12}=-(2+4)=-6,\quad C_{13}=1-4=-3$$

$$C_{21}=-(-2-1)=3,\quad C_{22}=4-4=0,\quad C_{23}=-(2+4)=-6$$

$$C_{31}=(1-1)=0,\quad C_{32}=-(-2-1)=3,\quad C_{33}=2+1=3$$

$$\text{adj}\,A=\begin{bmatrix}3&3&0\\-6&0&3\\-3&-6&3\end{bmatrix}$$

$$A^{-1}=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}3&3&0\\-6&0&3\\-3&-6&3\end{bmatrix}$$

$$X=A^{-1}B=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}3&3&0\\-6&0&3\\-3&-6&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\7\end{bmatrix}=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}6+3+0\\-12+0+21\\-6-6+21\end{bmatrix}=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}9\\9\\9\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore\ x=1,\ y=1,\ z=1$$

**Check:** $2-1+1=2$ ✓; $1+1-1=1$ ✓; $4+1+2=7$ ✓.

questions.topic: Tangent and Normal to a Parametric Curve
questions.question: Find the equations of the tangent and normal to the curve $x=\sin3t$, $y=\cos2t$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — the point.** At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$$x_1=\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\qquad y_1=\cos\frac{2\pi}{4}=\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0$$

So the point of contact is $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\ 0\right)$.

**Step 2 — the slope.** Differentiate parametrically:

$$\frac{dx}{dt}=3\cos3t,\qquad \frac{dy}{dt}=-2\sin2t$$

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\frac{-2\sin2t}{3\cos3t}$$

At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$: $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1$ and $\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so

$$\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{t=\pi/4}=\frac{-2(1)}{3\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)}=\frac{-2}{-\frac{3}{\sqrt2}}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$$

**Step 3 — tangent.** Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$:

$$y-0=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\left(x-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)$$

$$y=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}x-\frac{2\sqrt2}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{tangent:}\quad y=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}$$

or in general form $2\sqrt2\,x-3y-2=0$.

**Step 4 — normal.** Its slope is the negative reciprocal, $-\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt2}$, so

$$y-0=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}\left(x-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)$$

$$y=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}x+\frac{3}{2\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2}=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}x+\frac34$$

$$\therefore\ \text{normal:}\quad y=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}x+\frac34$$

or $3x+2\sqrt2\,y-\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}=0$ after clearing denominators.

**Check:** the two slopes multiply to $\dfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt2}\right)=-1$ ✓, as tangent and normal must be perpendicular.

questions.topic: Area of a Triangle by Integration
questions.question: Using integration, find the area of the triangle whose vertices are $(1,3)$, $(2,5)$ and $(3,4)$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — equations of the sides.** Using the two-point form $y-y_1=\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}(x-x_1)$:

**Side AB** through $(1,3)$ and $(2,5)$:

$$y-3=\frac{5-3}{2-1}(x-1)=2(x-1)$$

$$y=2x+1\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**Side BC** through $(2,5)$ and $(3,4)$:

$$y-5=\frac{4-5}{3-2}(x-2)=-(x-2)$$

$$y=-x+7\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Side AC** through $(1,3)$ and $(3,4)$:

$$y-3=\frac{4-3}{3-1}(x-1)=\frac12(x-1)$$

$$y=\frac{x}{2}+\frac52\qquad\ldots(3)$$

**Step 2 — split the region.** For $x$ from $1$ to $2$ the upper boundary is $AB$ and the lower is $AC$; for $x$ from $2$ to $3$ the upper boundary is $BC$ and the lower is again $AC$. (The point $(2,5)$ is the peak, so the upper boundary changes there.)

**Area ADB** ($1\le x\le2$):

$$A_1=\int_1^2\left[(2x+1)-\left(\frac x2+\frac52\right)\right]dx=\int_1^2\left(\frac{3x}{2}-\frac32\right)dx$$

$$=\frac32\int_1^2(x-1)\,dx=\frac32\left[\frac{(x-1)^2}{2}\right]_1^2=\frac32\cdot\frac12=\frac34$$

**Area BDC** ($2\le x\le3$):

$$A_2=\int_2^3\left[(-x+7)-\left(\frac x2+\frac52\right)\right]dx=\int_2^3\left(-\frac{3x}{2}+\frac92\right)dx$$

$$=\frac32\int_2^3(3-x)\,dx=\frac32\left[-\frac{(3-x)^2}{2}\right]_2^3=\frac32\cdot\frac12=\frac34$$

**Step 3 — total area.**

$$A=A_1+A_2=\frac34+\frac34=\frac32$$

$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\frac32\ \text{square units}$$

**Check by the shoelace formula:** with $(1,3),(2,5),(3,4)$,

$$\text{Area}=\frac12\left|1(5-4)+2(4-3)+3(3-5)\right|=\frac12\left|1+2-6\right|=\frac12(3)=\frac32\ \checkmark$$

questions.question: Verify that $y=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$ is a solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}-2\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=0$. / Or, solve $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-x\tan\dfrac yx$.
questions.answer:
**First part — verification.** Given

$$y=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)\qquad\ldots(1)$$

**First derivative** (product rule):

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=e^x(\cos x-\sin x)+e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$$

$$=e^x\left(\cos x-\sin x+\sin x+\cos x\right)=2e^x\cos x$$

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=2e^x\cos x\qquad\ldots(2)$$

**Second derivative:**

$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2\left[e^x\cos x+e^x(-\sin x)\right]=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)$$

$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)\qquad\ldots(3)$$

**Substitute into the left-hand side:**

$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-2\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)-2\left(2e^x\cos x\right)+2e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$$

$$=e^x\left[2\cos x-2\sin x-4\cos x+2\sin x+2\cos x\right]$$

$$=e^x\left[2\cos x-4\cos x+2\cos x-2\sin x+2\sin x\right]=e^x(0)=0$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-2\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=0\qquad\blacksquare$$

So $y=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)$ is indeed a solution.

**Or — the homogeneous equation.** Divide $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y-x\tan\dfrac yx$ by $x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac yx-\tan\frac yx$$

This is homogeneous of degree 0. Put $y=vx$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}$:

$$v+x\frac{dv}{dx}=v-\tan v$$

$$x\frac{dv}{dx}=-\tan v$$

**Separate the variables:**

$$\frac{dv}{\tan v}=-\frac{dx}{x}\ \Rightarrow\ \cot v\,dv=-\frac{dx}{x}$$

**Integrate:**

$$\int\cot v\,dv=-\int\frac{dx}{x}$$

$$\log(\sin v)=-\log x+\log c$$

$$\log(\sin v)+\log x=\log c\ \Rightarrow\ \log(x\sin v)=\log c$$

$$x\sin v=c$$

**Back-substitute $v=\dfrac yx$:**

$$x\sin\frac yx=c$$

$$\therefore\ x\sin\dfrac{y}{x}=c$$

which is the required general solution (equivalently $\sin\dfrac yx=\dfrac cx$).

questions.question: Consider the equations of the straight lines $L_1:\vec r=\left(\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k\right)+\lambda\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)$ and $L_2:\vec r=\left(2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k\right)+\mu\left(2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\right)$. If $\vec a_1=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b_1=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec a_2=2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec b_2=2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$, then find (i) $\vec a_2-\vec a_1$ (ii) $\vec b_2-\vec b_1$ (iii) $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$ (iv) $\vec a_1\times\vec a_2$ (v) $\left(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right)\cdot\left(\vec a_2-\vec a_1\right)$ (vi) the shortest distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\vec a_2-\vec a_1$:**

$$\vec a_2-\vec a_1=\left(2\hat i-\hat j-\hat k\right)-\left(\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k\right)=\hat i-3\hat j-2\hat k$$

**(ii) $\vec b_2-\vec b_1$:**

$$\vec b_2-\vec b_1=\left(2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\right)-\left(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\right)=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$$

**(iii) $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$:**

$$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-1&1\\2&1&2\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(-1)(2)-(1)(1)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(2)-(1)(2)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(1)-(-1)(2)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(-2-1)-\hat j(2-2)+\hat k(1+2)$$

$$=-3\hat i-0\hat j+3\hat k=-3\hat i+3\hat k$$

**(iv) $\vec a_1\times\vec a_2$:**

$$\vec a_1\times\vec a_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&2&1\\2&-1&-1\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(2)(-1)-(1)(-1)\right]-\hat j\left[(1)(-1)-(1)(2)\right]+\hat k\left[(1)(-1)-(2)(2)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(-2+1)-\hat j(-1-2)+\hat k(-1-4)$$

$$=-\hat i+3\hat j-5\hat k$$

**(v) The scalar triple product:**

$$\left(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right)\cdot\left(\vec a_2-\vec a_1\right)=(-3\hat i+0\hat j+3\hat k)\cdot(\hat i-3\hat j-2\hat k)$$

$$=(-3)(1)+(0)(-3)+(3)(-2)=-3+0-6=-9$$

So the triple product is $-9$.

**(vi) Shortest distance between the lines:**

$$d=\frac{\left|\left(\vec a_2-\vec a_1\right)\cdot\left(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right)\right|}{\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|}=\frac{\left|-9\right|}{\sqrt{9+0+9}}=\frac{9}{\sqrt{18}}=\frac{9}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}$$

$$\therefore\ d=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\ \text{units}\approx2.121$$

**Step-by-step:** the distance between skew lines is the projection of the vector joining a point on each line onto the common normal $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$; here that normal has length $3\sqrt2$ and the projection is $9$, giving $\dfrac{9}{3\sqrt2}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt2}$.

questions.question: A manufacturer has three machine operators A, B and C. A produces 1% defective items, while B and C produce 5% and 7% defective items respectively. A is on the job 50% of the time, B 30% and C 20%. Let $E_1$ be the event that an item is produced by A, $E_2$ by B and $E_3$ by C, and let E be the event that a defective item is produced. Find (i) $P(E_1)$ (ii) $P(E_2)$ (iii) $P(E_3)$ (iv) $P(E/E_1)$ (v) $P(E/E_2)$ (vi) $P(E_1/E)$.
questions.answer:
**The given data.**

$$P(E_1)=50\%=0.5,\qquad P(E_2)=30\%=0.3,\qquad P(E_3)=20\%=0.2$$

The conditional probabilities of a defective item from each operator are

$$P(E/E_1)=1\%=0.01,\qquad P(E/E_2)=5\%=0.05,\qquad P(E/E_3)=7\%=0.07$$

**(i), (ii), (iii) The prior probabilities** are read directly:

$$P(E_1)=0.5,\qquad P(E_2)=0.3,\qquad P(E_3)=0.2$$

(Note $0.5+0.3+0.2=1$ ✓ — the three operators exhaust all production.)

**(iv), (v) The conditional probabilities:**

$$P(E/E_1)=\frac{1}{100}=0.01,\qquad P(E/E_2)=\frac{5}{100}=0.05$$

**(vi) $P(E_1/E)$ — Bayes' theorem.** First find the total probability of a defective item:

$$P(E)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}P(E_i)\,P(E/E_i)$$

$$=0.5(0.01)+0.3(0.05)+0.2(0.07)$$

$$=0.005+0.015+0.014=0.034$$

$$P(E)=\frac{34}{1000}=\frac{17}{500}$$

Now

$$P\left(\frac{E_1}{E}\right)=\frac{P(E_1)\,P(E/E_1)}{P(E)}=\frac{0.005}{0.034}=\frac{5}{34}$$

$$\therefore\ P\left(\frac{E_1}{E}\right)=\frac{5}{34}\approx0.147$$

**Interpretation:** although A makes half the items, only $\dfrac{5}{34}$ of all defectives come from A — because A's defect rate (1%) is much lower than B's (5%) and C's (7%). The remaining $\dfrac{15}{34}$ and $\dfrac{14}{34}$ come from B and C.

questions.question: Solve graphically the following L.P.P.: Minimise $Z=5x+10y$ subject to $x+y\ge60$, $x+2y\le120$, $x-2y\ge0$, $x,y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — draw the boundary lines.**

$$x+y=60:\ \text{intercepts }(60,0),(0,60)$$

$$x+2y=120:\ \text{intercepts }(120,0),(0,60)$$

$$x-2y=0:\ \text{i.e. } x=2y,\ \text{the line through the origin with slope }\tfrac12$$

**Step 2 — decide the feasible side of each line.**

- $x+y\ge60$: the region **above** the line (the origin gives $0<60$, so the origin side is excluded).
- $x+2y\le120$: the region **below** the line (the origin satisfies it).
- $x-2y\ge0$: the region where $x\ge2y$ — to the **right/below** the line $x=2y$ (the origin is on the line, and test points like $(10,1)$ satisfy $10\ge2$).
- $x,y\ge0$: the first quadrant.

The feasible region is the quadrilateral **ABCD** with the vertices found below.

**Step 3 — the vertices.**

**A:** where $x+y=60$ meets the $x$-axis ($y=0$): $x=60$. So $A(60,0)$.

**B:** where $x+y=60$ meets $x=2y$: substituting $x=2y$ gives $2y+y=60\Rightarrow3y=60\Rightarrow y=20,\ x=40$. So $B(40,20)$ — actually the intersection of $x+y=60$ and $x-2y=0$, labelled D in the booklet's figure.

**C:** where $x+2y=120$ meets $x=2y$: $2y+2y=120\Rightarrow4y=120\Rightarrow y=30,\ x=60$. So $C(60,30)$.

**D:** where $x+2y=120$ meets the $x$-axis: $x=120$. So $D(120,0)$.

Taking the corners of the feasible quadrilateral as the booklet does — $A(60,0)$, $B(40,20)$, $C(60,30)$ and the point $B'(120,0)$ — the constraint $x-2y\ge0$ actually cuts the region at $x=2y$, so the feasible vertices are $(60,0)$, $(40,20)$ and $(60,30)$.

**Step 4 — evaluate $Z=5x+10y$.**

| Vertex | $Z=5x+10y$ |
|---|---|
| $(60,0)$ | $5(60)+0=300$ |
| $(40,20)$ | $5(40)+10(20)=200+200=400$ |
| $(60,30)$ | $5(60)+10(30)=300+300=600$ |

**Step 5 — conclusion.** The smallest value is

$$Z_{\min}=300$$

attained at

$$x=60,\qquad y=0$$

$$\therefore\ Z_{\min}=5(60)+10(0)=300\ \text{at the point }(60,0)$$

Since the objective $Z=5x+10y$ increases most steeply in the $y$-direction and $y$ is minimised at $y=0$ along the feasible boundary, the minimum sits at the corner $(60,0)$ — matching the booklet's answer of 300 at point A.
